Partner and Roommate Compatibility

White noise wins here, almost every time. It's consistent, predictable, and easy to tune out if you're not the one who needs it. ASMR is variable. A whisperer who suddenly shifts tone, a sound that repeats unexpectedly, a role-play scenario that starts mid-sentence. That variability is what makes it effective for the listener. It's also exactly what makes it irritating for anyone else in the room.

If you share a sleep space, use white noise through a speaker so it benefits both of you, and run your ASMR through earbuds if you need it. Wireless earbuds designed for side-sleeping exist and are worth the investment if this is a regular issue.

The compromise that actually works: white noise at a moderate volume as the shared baseline, ASMR for the person who needs it at low volume through one earbud. You get the variability that triggers your response. They get the consistent mask that doesn't pull their attention.

Travel and Hotel Use: Which Works Better

Unfamiliar environments are harder to sleep in because your brain stays partly alert to new sounds. Hotel hallways, street noise, HVAC systems that cycle on and off. These are exactly the conditions where the consistent masking of white noise outperforms ASMR.

ASMR in a hotel can backfire. The variable sounds can highlight the gaps where the unfamiliar room sounds are still getting through. White noise fills those gaps completely.

The practical recommendation for travel: use brown noise as your base through a travel speaker, not your phone speaker. If you find you still need ASMR to actually relax, run it very quietly through earbuds underneath the brown noise. The brown noise handles the masking job. The ASMR handles the relaxation. You're not asking either to do the other's job.
